q: A Fino goes into bottle with little more than a coarse filter, released in small lots in spring and again in autumn. What has the guest gained, and lost?
opts: A higher strength, the wine having been fortified a second time on its way into the bottle
More of the veil's yeasty, saline intensity, and much less time before the bottle tires
Residual sweetness, some of the sugar having been left unfermented
A deeper colour and walnut character, the wine having oxidised for years after its flor died
exp: Cold stabilisation and tight filtration strip fine solids that carry aroma, so leaving them in gives a fuller and more savoury wine that is also markedly less stable. The release dates are not marketing: the veil is thickest in spring and autumn and thinnest in the heat of August, so the wine underneath is genuinely different at different times of year.

q: At the first classification the capataz chalks a mark on the butt, and one mark sends the young wine down the biological road. Name that mark.
exp: A stroke like a palm frond says the wine is delicate and clean and will be lightly fortified to keep its veil alive. A raya, a plain horizontal bar, sends a fuller wine the oxidative way, and the crossed mark that gives Palo Cortado its name is a palma struck through, meaning the cellar master changed his mind about it.

q: Before the letters VORS may go on a label the regulating body verifies the claimed average age in a laboratory rather than from the cellar book. Which test does it use?
exp: Atmospheric nuclear testing left a spike of radiocarbon in everything grown since the 1950s, and the amount left in a wine gives its age directly, which no ledger could prove for a blend that has never been a single vintage. VOS claims an average of twenty years and VORS thirty, and both are checked this way before the seal is granted.

q: Zoning came to Cava so that a label could finally say where the fruit grew rather than only how the wine was made. Which is a genuine Cava zone?
opts: Comtats de Barcelona
Ribera del Cava
Camp de Tarragona
Alt Penedes
exp: The denomination was drawn around a production method and a register of approved plots rather than around a boundary, which is how it came to stretch across half the country, and the zones answer the old complaint that followed from it. A buyer can now tell an Ebro valley bottle from a Catalan one, and a zone may be subdivided further so a district can be named as well.

q: Cava's ageing tiers were sorted into two families, the upper one vintage-dated and starting at eighteen months on the lees. Name that upper family.
exp: Reserva, Gran Reserva and the single-plot tier all sit inside it, and every wine in the family must declare its harvest year, which the entry tier below need not. Because the family carries the vintage, a bottle without one is telling a buyer where it sits without ever printing the word.

q: The oldest Basque txakoli denomination is named for a fishing town on the Gipuzkoa coast. Name that denomination.
exp: Recognised at the end of the 1980s, it covers the steep coastal slopes either side of the town and is the most maritime of the three Basque denominations. The others cover Bizkaia around Bilbao and Araba inland in the Ayala valley, sheltered behind the Sierra Salvada but still on the Atlantic side of the watershed, where the wines are riper and a good deal less salty.

q: Txakoli is nearly all white, yet the Basque rulebooks also list a black-berried variety for the rare reds and rosados. Name it.
exp: Beltza is Basque for black, and the grape is a small share of the plantings; a little is co-fermented with the white in some villages to give the pink wine its colour. Both varieties trail their canopies on high pergolas above the damp ground, which is the same answer to the same problem the Galicians reached on the other end of the same coast.

q: A pet-nat maker wants a gentle two and a half bar in the finished wine rather than a spumante's six. Where is that decision actually made?
opts: On bottling day, in how much unfermented sugar is still in the wine as it goes under the cap
At disgorgement, where pressure is vented along with the frozen plug of sediment
In the cellar's temperature, cold storage setting how much carbon dioxide the finished wine holds
In the liqueur de tirage, by cutting back the sugar and yeast added for the second fermentation
exp: An ancestral wine has one fermentation and nothing is ever added to provoke another, so the only gas it will ever hold comes from whatever sugar the ferment has not yet eaten when the wine goes into glass. Each four grams or so per litre finishes into roughly one further atmosphere, which is why the style sits naturally at modest pressures and often keeps a touch of sweetness: the tail of a chilled ferment rarely eats the bottle dry. There is no tirage liqueur to adjust and frequently no disgorgement either, so the maker's whole control is the timing of that one bottling.

q: Two American sparklers stand together: the back of one reads fermented in this bottle, the other only bottle fermented. What is the shorter phrase quietly admitting?
opts: The second fermentation ran in a sealed tank and the wine was bottled under counter-pressure
Nothing; American labelling treats the phrases as interchangeable
The wine left the bottle it fermented in, finished in tank and rebottled: the transfer method
The bubble was injected on the bottling line, as it would be into a soft drink
exp: American convention reserves fermented in THIS bottle for wine sold in the glass it refermented in, while plain bottle fermented covers transfer wine, which took its bubble and its lees character in bottle and was then emptied under pressure, filtered, dosed and refilled in one batch operation. The economics are the point: the whole run is cleaned up in tank instead of being riddled and disgorged a bottle at a time. The label wording is often the only clue a buyer gets.

q: Five years on from a shared disgorging date, a Brut and its Brut Nature sibling taste further apart than a few grams of sugar explain. What has the dosage been doing all that time?
opts: Nothing beyond sweetness; sugar is inert once dissolved, and the gap is the tasters' expectation
Reacting slowly with what the yeast left behind, steering the dosed wine toward toast and roast
Feeding a refermentation that has quietly raised the dosed bottle's pressure
Fermenting out, so the Brut has been drifting toward its sibling's dryness
exp: Dosage sugar is not inert: over years in bottle it takes part in slow browning chemistry with the nitrogen compounds autolysis left in the wine, and that pushes development toward the roasted, toasted register. The undosed wine ages along a leaner, more saline road rather than simply tasting less sweet, which is why houses speak of dosage needing time to marry and why the choice between the two styles is a choice of trajectory, not just of sugar.

q: Spumante on an Italian label is a legal claim about pressure, not a style note, and there is a floor the dissolved gas must clear. Give that floor.
exp: Three bar of overpressure at twenty degrees is where European law draws the line for a fully sparkling wine, with frizzante occupying the band from one to two and a half. The quality-sparkling category that most Cremant and metodo classico wines sit in actually demands slightly more, three and a half, so a wine at three point two can be spumante and still fail that tier. Below one bar the law reads the wine as still, whatever prickle it shows.

q: Under one bar of pressure French law reads a wine as still, yet lists and back labels keep a word for that faint natural prick in the glass. Give the word.
exp: Perlant sits below petillant on the old French ladder: petillant carries a real if gentle sparkle in the one to two and a half bar band, while perlant is barely a whisper of gas, the sort a Muscadet bottled on its lees keeps from the winter's fermentation. The word makes no legal promise at all, which is exactly the point: it names a sensation the law has stopped measuring.

q: Hambledon's 1950s replanting and most English vineyards for the next four decades leaned on German crossings plus one French-bred hybrid hardy enough for the climate. Which hybrid?
opts: Baco Noir
Seyval Blanc
Vidal Blanc
Villard Blanc
exp: Seyval Blanc, a Seyve-Villard cross, carried the acidity and rot resistance a cold wet season demands and made respectable bottle-fermented wine at estates like Breaky Bottom. Its hybrid parentage kept it outside the European quality-wine categories, which is one reason the industry swung so hard to Chardonnay and the Pinots once the warming climate let them ripen.

q: One English county's name has stood since 2022 as a protected wine origin in its own right, the first drawn at county scale. Which county?
opts: Cornwall
Essex
Hampshire
Sussex
exp: The Sussex PDO took seven years from application to grant and binds its users more tightly than the countrywide English designation, including the traditional method for its sparkling wine. The argument it caused was less about the rules than the map: fruit and presses cross the county line constantly, and growers elsewhere have so far preferred the broader name.

q: Most of England's vineyard crowds into the southeastern corner, where the Downs run their chalk toward the Channel, and adjoining counties there hold the bulk of it. Name the pair.
exp: Kent and Sussex between them hold the largest share of the national vineyard, with Hampshire next and Essex climbing fastest on its warm clay. The chalk gets the attention, but a surprising number of well-regarded sites actually sit on greensand, so the county and the rock are separate claims and a label naming one is not promising the other.

q: In 1988 a West Sussex estate planted Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier and nothing else, a bet on the traditional method made while nearly every English vine was a crossing or a hybrid. Name the estate.
exp: Its first releases in the mid-1990s took national trophies and did more than any argument on paper to turn the industry toward the Champagne varieties. The founding vineyards sit on greensand rather than the chalk the region is celebrated for, a useful correction to the idea that England's case rests on chalk alone, and the name itself belongs to a manor recorded in Domesday.
